title: How UK PhD Funding Actually Works: DTPs, CDTs and Doctoral Landscape Awards
seoTitle: UK PhD Funding Explained: DTP, CDT and Doctoral Landscape Awards
seoDescription: How UKRI training grants become funded PhD projects: DLA, DTP and CDT routes, who pays what, when rounds open, and how to apply for a fully funded UK studentship.
intro: Most 'fully funded PhD in the UK' adverts you see are ultimately paid for by one source: UKRI training grants. Understanding how that money reaches a project explains almost everything about how to win one.

content:
Scroll through UK PhD adverts and you will meet the same alphabet soup everywhere: DTP, CDT, DLA, CDA. They are not competing funders. They are different plumbing through which the same pot of money — mostly UK Research and Innovation training grants — reaches an individual funded project. Once you see the system from the funder's side, choosing where to apply gets much easier.

The money's journey: UKRI to university to you

UKRI does not award PhD studentships to individuals. It awards large multi-year training grants to universities and consortia, who then create funded studentships: one stipend at the UKRI minimum rate, plus tuition fees at the minimum fee level, plus a research and training support grant for your consumables, conferences and fieldwork. Your job as an applicant is to find the projects these grants have created and compete for them — which is why every advert says "apply to the project", never "apply to UKRI".

DLA, DTP and CDT: what the letters mean now

Since 2025/26, UKRI's main investment is the Doctoral Landscape Award (DLA), which absorbed and aligned the older Doctoral Training Partnerships (DTPs) and similar partnership schemes. Most councils still run their DLAs through existing partnership structures, so you will see "DTP" and "DLA" used almost interchangeably on university pages for the next few years. A DLA typically funds a cohort of students across a discipline area — ESRC DLAs in the social sciences, EPSRC DLAs in engineering and physics, AHRC DLAs in the arts and humanities, and so on.

Centres for Doctoral Training (CDTs) are the team-sport version. A CDT recruits a cohort that starts together, usually takes taught modules and a rotation project in year one, and only then settles on a thesis. CDTs are common in AI and robotics, quantum technologies, manufacturing and materials — fields where cohort training and industry contact matter. If you are an international applicant, note that CDTs and DLAs recruit on project merit rather than country quota, and international students do win these studentships regularly, but fees funding for international applicants varies by award, so always read the funding line rather than assuming home-fee terms.

When rounds open and close

The rhythm is mostly annual and mostly autumn. Universities advertise projects between August and November, deadlines cluster between October and January, interviews follow in the new year, and funded places start the following September or October. Some councils run fixed competitions — AHRC Doctoral Landscape Awards at several universities close in early winter, while EPSRC-linked CDTs often run rolling shortlists. Because every consortium sets its own dates, the practical approach is to track the projects: our Edinburgh AI CDT listing and Kent AHRC DLA listing show how differently two DLAs can schedule the same season.

What else funds UK PhDs

UKRI money is the backbone but not the whole skeleton. Charities such as Wellcome and Cancer Research UK fund biomedical studentships at rates above the UKRI floor. Individual universities run scholarship schemes of their own — College Research Awards, Presidential Scholarships, Vice-Chancellor awards — which are funded from institutional pots rather than training grants. Medical charities, the Royal Academy of Engineering, and partner-organisations under CASE-style co-funding add further routes. And for UK-home students who would rather borrow than compete, the Postgraduate Doctoral Loan offers a non-competitive fallback of up to £31,122.

How to pick between them

If you know your research area precisely, apply to named projects — they are usually better funded and faster to assess. If you know your field but not your question, a CDT or DLA cohort gives you a year to find your thesis and often better industry links. If you need maximum flexibility on topic, university scholarship schemes tend to leave the research question to you. Most successful applicants do all three at once: three named projects, one cohort scheme and one university award is a normal autumn workload, and it costs nothing but time to apply broadly.

Reading a studentship advert like a funder

Adverts hide their funding source in plain sight, and it changes what you can negotiate. A project that says "fully funded for home and international students" with fees at the UKRI minimum and a stipend at £21,805 is UKRI money and the terms are fixed. A project offering "fees only" or a partial stipend is usually a university or charity pot, and there is sometimes room to stack a second award. An advert that mentions "industry partner" often carries a top-up and better internship access. Check three lines before applying: the funding type, who is eligible (home-only awards waste an international applicant's time), and whether the deadline is a fixed competition or a rolling shortlist.

Timing your application matters as much as choosing it. The strongest applications arrive early in the window with a supervisor already aware of your name from an email exchange; our templates for emailing UK supervisors exist precisely for that first contact. And if you are deciding between a cohort CDT and a named project, think honestly about how you work — cohorts suit people who want structure and peers, named projects suit people who already know their thesis question.

See the three models live: DTP, CDT and DLA listings

The funding alphabet only makes sense once you see real examples. Each card below is a live example of one of the three routes — open a few and you will spot the pattern in how they describe projects, training and deadlines.

  • ESRC White Rose DTP Studentships 2027/28 at the University of Leeds — one of the largest ESRC Doctoral Training Partnerships. Deadline: 17:00 (UK Time) 20 January 2027.
  • Sensor Technologies and Applications CDT PhD, Cambridge 2027 — Cambridge's Sensor Technologies CDT. Deadline: 6 January 2027 (funding deadline).
  • AI for Biomedical Innovation CDT at University of Edinburgh 2027 — an AI-for-biomedicine CDT at Edinburgh. Deadline: 20 January 2027, 13:00 UK.
  • Net Zero Futures Doctoral Landscape Award, Royal College of Art — a design-led Doctoral Landscape Award at the Royal College of Art. Deadline: 2027 call deadline not yet announced.
  • EPSRC DLA PhD: Decision-Theoretic Shared-Autonomy for Remote Robotics at Lancaster University — a rolling EPSRC DLA studentship in shared-autonomy robotics at Lancaster
